title: Nobody Can Stop a Man Who's Done the Inner Work | 8 Truths About Unshakable Confidence
fullText: Let me ask you something. >> [music] >> Think about the last time someone talked down to you. Maybe it was a co-worker who took credit for your idea in a meeting. >> [music] >> Maybe it was someone you trusted who used your vulnerabilities against you. Maybe it was a friend who stopped calling the moment your situation stopped being useful to them. >> [music] >> Now, here is the real question. What did you do? Did you confront it? Did [music] you go home and rehearse the perfect response in your head for the next 3 hours? Did you [music] tell yourself you were being too sensitive? Let it slide and keep showing up like nothing happened? >> [music] >> Most people go with that last option. And [clears throat] I understand why. We have been trained from childhood to believe that peacekeeping is a virtue. That tolerating bad behavior is a form of grace. That being the bigger person means absorbing whatever someone throws at you with a smile on your face. But here is what nobody tells you. There is a difference between being gracious and being a doormat. There is a difference between choosing your battles and [music] refusing to acknowledge that a war is being waged against your dignity. Today, I want to give you eight truths. >> [music] >> Not motivational fluff. Not recycled positivity. Eight actual [music] practical truths about how power works, how people operate, and how to build the kind of internal foundation that nobody can shake. [music] These truths are uncomfortable. Some of them will challenge beliefs you have held your whole life. But if you stay with me, >> [music] >> by the time we are done, you will see yourself and the world around you completely differently. Let us get into it. Truth one. You were not born passive. >> [music] >> You were trained to be. Here is something worth sitting with. You were not always the person who hesitates to speak up. You were not always the one who says sorry automatically, >> [music] >> even when you did nothing wrong. You were not born second-guessing yourself. That was learned. Think about how children operate before the world gets to them. They are honest. [music] They say what they want. They push back when something does not feel right. They have no filter for self-doubt because nobody has installed one yet. Then, life starts installing it. Your parents, with the best intentions in the world, started correcting you. Do not be too loud. Do not be so demanding. Share even when you do not want to. >> [music] >> Be polite even to people who are rude to you. And on some level, all of that is reasonable. But taken too far, what it [music] creates is an adult who has been so thoroughly trained to suppress their instincts that they no longer know what those instincts are. School reinforced it. Raise your hand. Wait your turn. Do not challenge authority. Conform to the structure. Fit the mold. Be easy to grade, easy to manage, easy to predict. And then the workplace continued it. Go along with things you disagree with. Do not rock the boat. Be a team player, which is often code for do not have too many opinions of your own. By the time most people are adults, they have [music] accumulated decades of conditioning that tells them that staying small is safe. That speaking up is risky. >> [music] >> That standing firm on what you believe is arrogance. It is not arrogance. It is self-respect. >> [music] >> And it is something you are going to have to consciously rebuild. The first step is simply awareness. Start noticing the moments when you shrink. When you apologize and you do not know why. When you change your answer because someone pushed back, not because they gave you a good reason, but because the social pressure made you uncomfortable. When you nod along in a conversation while something inside you is screaming that you disagree. Notice it. Do not judge [music] it. Just see it clearly because you cannot change what you are unwilling to acknowledge. And once you start seeing the pattern, >> [music] >> you can start interrupting it. You were not born this way. You were conditioned this way. Which means you can recondition yourself. Truth two. Your mind is either your greatest asset or your most dangerous enemy. Here is [music] a test. Think of something difficult that happened to you recently. A conflict. A setback. [music] A moment of rejection or disappointment. Now, ask yourself. How long did you spend thinking about it afterward? [music] If the answer is hours or days or weeks, you are not alone. Most people do this. >> [music] >> They replay events on a loop. They analyze every word. They construct elaborate alternate scenarios where they said the right thing, >> [music] >> did the right thing, and came out on top. And all of that mental energy goes absolutely nowhere except [music] deeper into anxiety and frustration. The problem is not that you have emotions. >> [music] >> The problem is that your emotions are running your operating system without your permission. Think of [clears throat] it this way. Your emotional response to any given situation is like a notification on your phone. It is useful information. It [music] is telling you that something happened. That something crossed a threshold. But if you let every notification pull you away from what you are doing, you will never get anything done. You will be at the mercy of whatever pings, whatever buzzes, whatever flares up in the moment. Mentally strong people do not ignore their emotions. They read them. When something makes you angry, the anger is telling you something. >> [music] >> It is telling you that a value got violated. That a boundary got crossed. >> [music] >> That something matters to you. That is useful data. But it does not mean the anger itself should be driving your next move. When something makes you anxious, the anxiety is pointing at something. >> [music] >> A risk you have not addressed. An uncertainty you have not resolved. Again [music] useful. But anxiety making decisions on your behalf >> [music] >> tends to produce bad outcomes. The goal is to build what I call mental distance. The ability to feel something fully and still choose how you respond [music] to it. This is a skill, not a personality trait. And you build it through practice. [music] When something triggers a strong emotional reaction in you, try this. Before you respond. Before you send the text. >> [music] >> Before you make the call. Before you say the thing that is sitting right on the tip of your tongue. Pause. >> [music] >> Even 30 seconds. Ask yourself. If I respond from this emotional state, what will the outcome likely be? Is that the outcome I want? More often than not, that pause alone will change your response entirely. The people who have the most influence in any [music] room are almost never the most reactive. They are the calmest. They are the ones who can sit with discomfort without visibly flinching. And that calm is not [music] a natural gift. It is a trained discipline. Train your mind. It will be the most valuable thing you ever do. Truth three. Silence is a strategy, not an absence. Here is something that tends to surprise people. Across every professional environment, every social dynamic, every negotiation table in America, the person who talks the least almost always holds the most perceived power. We have this cultural instinct, especially in America, to fill silence. [music] We are conditioned to believe that silence is awkward. That it signals weakness. That talking more equals showing more value. So, [music] we overexplain. We justify decisions nobody asked us to justify. We argue our case long after the argument is over. >> [music] >> And every word we add after the point has been made costs us something. Think about the strongest people you have encountered in your life. The ones whose opinion you genuinely respected. The ones who, when they said something, it actually landed. I am willing to bet that those people were not the loudest in the room. They were selective, precise. [music] When they spoke, it meant something. That is not an accident. That is a discipline. Silence does several powerful things that most people underestimate. First, it makes you unreadable. When someone cannot easily predict what you are thinking or feeling, they pay closer attention. They stop taking you for granted. Mystery, [music] even the mild kind, commands respect in a way that oversharing never will. Second [music] silence protects you. You cannot be held accountable for something you never said. You cannot be quoted out of context, [music] twisted, or misrepresented if you were not speaking in the first place. The more you talk, especially in high-stakes situations, >> [music] >> the more you expose. Third, and maybe most importantly, silence gives you information. When you stop talking, other people [clears throat] start. And what they say when they fill that space tells you everything. Their insecurities come out. Their real intentions surface. Their assumptions about you reveal themselves. >> [music] >> The person who is comfortable with silence is almost always walking away from every conversation knowing more than the person who did all the talking. This does not mean become cold or checked out. It [music] means become intentional. Ask yourself before you speak. Does this add something? Does saying this move the conversation toward where I want it to go? Or am I just talking to manage my own discomfort? If the answer is the latter, stay quiet. [music] Let the silence do its work. You will be amazed at what it does. Truth four. [music] Disappointment is data, not devastation. One of the most painful and universal human experiences >> [music] >> is being let down by someone you trusted. And in America, where we are raised on ideals of loyalty, meritocracy, and fairness, [music] the disappointment often feels personal in a way that is genuinely destabilizing. He was my best friend for 15 years. >> [music] >> She was the one I went to bat for. I gave them every opportunity, and this [music] is how they repay me. Sound familiar? Here is what I want to offer you. >> [music] >> Not to make light of it, but to reframe it in a way that actually serves you. Disappointment is not a verdict on your worth. [music] It is information about someone else's character, priorities, and limitations. That is all it is. The problem is that we treat it like it is about us, when most of the time >> [music] >> it has almost nothing to do with us at all. People make choices based on what serves them in that [music] moment. That is human nature. It is not evil. It is not a conspiracy against you. >> [music] >> It is just what people do, and the sooner you understand that most of what others do is about their own situation and not yours, the less their choices will feel like personal attacks. >> [music] >> Now, that does not mean you accept every disappointment and move on without consequence. [music] Some disappointments are deal-breakers. Some people need to be removed from your circle permanently, not out of bitterness, but out of basic self-preservation. [music] Distance is sometimes the most rational and self-respecting response you can give, but the difference between a person who grows from disappointment and a person who gets destroyed by it is simple. One turns it into information. The other turns it into identity. The person who gets destroyed asks, >> [music] >> "Why would they do this to me? What is wrong with me that people keep letting me down?" >> [music] >> And they spiral into self-doubt and closed-off bitterness. The person who grows asks, "What does this tell me about this person? What did I miss? What do I now know that I did not know before?" And they adjust. They become more discerning. They invest more carefully. They build better judgment. Every disappointing situation, if you are willing to examine it honestly, >> [music] >> teaches you something that you could not have learned any other way. That is the gift buried inside [music] every letdown. You just have to be willing to look for it instead of letting the pain take [music] over. Use your disappointments. Let them sharpen you. Let them refine your instincts about people. Let them make you more selective, not more [music] guarded. There is a difference. Guarded people let nobody in. Selective people let the right people in. Become selective. Truth five, results are the only argument worth having. Let me paint you a picture. >> [music] >> Someone talks behind your back, spreads a narrative about you that is unfair, >> [music] >> incomplete, or just flat-out wrong. You find out about it. Your first instinct is to confront it, set the record straight, make sure everyone knows the truth. >> [music] >> I understand that instinct, but I want to challenge it because here is what happens when you argue against criticism directly. >> [music] >> You elevate it. You give it oxygen. You essentially announce that it has affected you, which [music] signals to the people watching that maybe there is something to it. Criticism that would have died quietly in a corner gets [music] dragged into the spotlight the moment you engage with it. The most effective response to doubt is not a counter-argument. >> [music] >> It is undeniable results. Think about the professionals, the entrepreneurs, >> [music] >> the leaders in this country who have built something genuinely significant. >> [music] >> They were talked about. They were doubted. People said they were too young, too inexperienced, too [music] naive, too ambitious, too different. And they responded by building something so obviously real that the criticism had nowhere to stand. That is the only argument that actually wins. Not the debate you have in the comment section. Not the conversation where you explain yourself. The work, the output, the track record. [music] This requires patience. It requires resisting the urge for immediate vindication because our culture is extremely dopamine-driven right now. >> [music] >> We want resolution fast. We want to correct the misunderstanding today, get the apology today, >> [music] >> feel vindicated today. And when that does not happen, it feels unbearable. But vindication through excellence is slow. >> [music] >> And it is the only kind that actually sticks. People who were laughed at and kept building are not remembered for the criticism. They are remembered for what they created. Nobody talks about who doubted them once the results are in. That is where you want to be. So, [music] the next time someone questions you, doubt you, dismiss you, resist the urge to debate them. Nod or say nothing >> [music] >> and go back to work. Let the work answer them. In time, and it will take time, the work always wins. >> [music] >> Truth six, your reputation is being built right now, whether you are intentional about it or not. Every interaction you have is building something. [music] Every time you show up early or late. Every time you follow through or fall short. >> [music] >> Every time you handle pressure with composure or with chaos. Every time you keep your word or quietly break it. All of it is accumulating into a reputation that precedes you. >> [music] >> Most people are completely passive about this. They assume their reputation just is what it is based on who they are, but that is not accurate. Your reputation is not just a reflection of your character. It is a reflection of how you have been perceived over time, across contexts, in moments of both comfort and stress, and you have far more control over it than you think. Start with consistency. >> [music] >> One of the most underrated qualities in any person, in any environment, is being the same person in every situation. When people know exactly what to expect from you, that predictability, in the [music] best sense of the word, becomes a form of trust. They know how you treat people below you because it is the same way you treat people above you. They know you will be direct >> [music] >> because you are always direct. They know you will deliver because you always deliver. Consistency [music] is what separates the people who have genuine reputations from the people who are just managing impressions. Then there is how you carry yourself physically. >> [music] >> This matters more than most people want to admit. How you walk into a room. How you hold yourself when you are standing still. How you make eye contact. [music] Whether you take up space or whether you contract yourself to be less noticeable. These physical signals communicate things about confidence, about presence, about self-concept before you have said a single word. >> [music] >> You do not have to be aggressive or imposing. You just have to be grounded. Move like you are exactly where you are supposed to be. >> [music] >> Speak at a pace that is unhurried. Listen without visibly rushing to jump in. Own the space you occupy. And then there is this. Be very selective about what you share, with whom, and when. [music] One of the fastest ways to damage your own reputation is oversharing. Sharing your plans before they are complete invites other people's doubt into your process. Sharing your vulnerabilities with people who have not earned that level of trust hands them a weapon. Sharing your grievances publicly, in the moment, before you have processed them, makes you look reactive and uncontrolled. Privacy is not the same as secrecy. >> [music] >> You are not hiding. You are protecting the things that matter to you until the time is right to reveal them. Control the story, not by being deceptive, but by being deliberate >> [music] >> because the narrative about who you are is going to be written. The only question is whether you are writing it or leaving [music] it to other people. Truth seven, discipline is the one thing nobody can take from [music] you. Every morning, before most of the country is awake, there are people in this country doing something hard. They are running when it is cold and dark and their body is saying, "Stay in bed." They are studying when the rest of their household is asleep. They are working on something that has no immediate payoff, no immediate recognition, no immediate reward. They are doing it anyway. These [music] are not superhuman people. They are not genetically gifted with extraordinary willpower. They are just people who made a decision at some point that their long-term trajectory matters more than their short-term comfort, and they make that decision again >> [music] >> every single day. Discipline is not a personality trait. It is a practice, and like every practice, >> [music] >> it gets easier with repetition. But here is what most people miss about discipline. They think it is about sacrifice, >> [music] >> about white-knuckling through things you hate, about suffering in the present for some hypothetical future reward. That [music] is not actually what it is. Real discipline is about building trust with yourself. Every time you say you are going to do something and you do [music] it, you are making a deposit into your own self-respect account. You are proving to yourself, in a small but real way, that your word means something, that you are someone who follows through, >> [music] >> that you can count on yourself. And over time, that compounding self-trust produces [music] something that no amount of external encouragement can manufacture. It produces genuine confidence. Not the kind that depends on other people affirming you. Not the kind that shatters when someone pushes back, >> [music] >> but the kind that is rooted in a long track record of keeping your own commitments. Start small, deliberately. Do not blow up your entire routine overnight and try to become a different person by next week. Pick one thing, >> [music] >> one commitment you make to yourself, and protect it like it matters because it does. Wake up at a consistent time every day for 30 days. Read for 30 minutes every morning. [music] Work on your project for 1 hour before you open your phone. >> [music] >> Whatever it is, make it specific. Make it manageable. And do not negotiate with yourself on it when the feeling to skip it shows up [music] because the feeling will show up every day, and every time you act anyway, despite the resistance, >> [music] >> you are building something in yourself that most people never develop, an inner authority, >> [music] >> a sense that you, and not your emotions or your circumstances, >> [music] >> are running the show. That is what nobody can take from you. Not your boss, not your critics, not economic downturns or bad luck or difficult seasons. Your discipline [music] belongs to you alone. Build it like it is the most important thing you own because in many ways, it is. [music] Truth eight, the life you want is built by becoming internally independent. >> [music] >> This is where everything we have talked about today converges. And I want to be honest with you about what internal independence actually [music] means because it gets misrepresented a lot. It does not mean becoming cold. >> [music] >> It does not mean refusing to love people or need people or let people in. Human connection is not a weakness. Loving people is not a vulnerability. >> [music] >> Community is not a crutch. Internal independence means that your peace, your identity, and your sense of direction are not outsourced to other people. [music] Here is what that looks like in practice. It means that when someone does not approve of your decision, you do not collapse. You listen. You consider whether there is something worth hearing. And then you proceed according to your own judgment. It means that when someone withdraws their affection or approval as a way to control you, >> [music] >> it does not work because you are not depending on their approval to feel okay about yourself in the first [music] place. It means that when you face a setback, your identity does not go down with it. You are not your job title. You are not your relationship status. [music] You are not your bank balance or your follower count or anyone else's opinion of your potential. Those things may change. Your [music] core does not have to. Most of the suffering that people experience in their day-to-day lives is not caused [music] by what is actually happening to them. It is caused by the gap between what is happening and what they think they need [music] in order to feel okay. And that gap is almost entirely created by dependence. Dependence on external circumstances to produce an internal state. When you do the work of building your own internal foundation, that gap starts to close. Not because life gets easier. >> [music] >> Life does not get easier. But because your ability to stand firm inside of whatever life brings you gets stronger. People will notice this shift in you. >> [music] >> They always do. Because people who are grounded react differently than people who are reactive. There is a steadiness to them that draws people in while simultaneously making it very difficult to manipulate or destabilize them. That is not an accident. That is the byproduct of someone who has done the real work on themselves. >> [music] >> You do not have to be the loudest. You do not have to be the most impressive. You do not have to have all the answers or project [music] false certainty or pretend that everything is fine when it is not. You just have to know who you are. And refuse to be argued out of it. When you know who you are, >> [music] >> you do not need to defend yourself constantly. You do not need to explain your choices to people who are not genuinely invested in [music] you. You do not need to earn your place in every room you walk into. You already have a place. You earned [music] it by doing the work. Let me take 60 seconds and walk back through what we covered today. >> [music] >> You were trained to be passive, not born that way. Which means the conditioning can be reversed. >> [music] >> You have the ability to reclaim the instincts and the directness that were gradually eroded out of you. Your mind is your primary tool. >> [music] >> Training it to process emotions without being ruled by them is not optional. It is the foundation of everything else. Silence is a strategy. Strategic, selective communication gives your words actual weight [music] and gives you real information from the people around you. Disappointment is information. People will let you down. This is not a crisis. It is data. >> [music] >> Use it to make better decisions going forward. Your results are your most powerful statement. Engaging with criticism directly gives it legitimacy. Building something undeniable makes it irrelevant. Your reputation is being [music] built right now. Consistency, composure, and intentional privacy are the tools. Use them deliberately. [music] Discipline is the one thing that is entirely yours. It is self-trust compounded daily. It produces the kind of confidence that no external force can manufacture or take [music] away. And internal independence is the destination. Not isolation. Not [music] coldness. But a grounded, rooted sense of self that does not need constant external validation to remain intact. Here is what I want to leave you with. The world has a way of finding your weakest point and pressing [music] on it. That is not a cynical observation. That is just the reality of a world full of people who are, most of the time, navigating their own insecurities and competing interests. >> [music] >> Your job is not to make the world stop pressing. Your job is to build something inside yourself [music] that does not give way when it does. That is the work. It is unglamorous. >> [music] >> It is slow. It is not the kind of thing that looks impressive on the outside while it is happening. But it is the only work that produces lasting results. You do not need anyone's permission to start. [music] You do not need ideal circumstances. You do not need to wait until you feel ready because that feeling is rarely coming on its own. You start today with one choice. To no longer hand over your peace, your power, or your direction to people and circumstances that have not earned that kind of authority over your life. One choice, then another, then another after that. >> [music] >> That is how it is built. And once it is built, it holds. Go do the work.
